abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Preclinical studies have evaluated murine double minue 2 (MDM2) inhibitors as a treatment for adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC), but clinical trials are lacking. This phase I trial (NCT03781986) assesses the safety and antitumor activity of an oral MDM2 inhibitor, alrizomadlin (APG-115), +/- carboplatin in TP53 wild type unresectable recurrent/metastatic salivary gland cancers (R/M SGC) with a planned 1:1 randomization to carboplatin chemotherapy. The co-primary endpoints are determination of dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) and response rate (RR) for alrizomadlin monotherapy +/- carboplatin. Secondary endpoints include safety, survival, and RR by tumor histology. After enrollment of 4 patients to combination therapy, the trial was modified to a single arm study of alrizomadlin monotherapy due to excess toxicity. 1 DLT was seen in the combination arm, all patients had ≥ G3 treatment related adverse events (TRAE). 37 patients were enrolled to alrizomadlin monotherapy. 3 DLTs were encountered, 67% of patients had ≥ G3 TRAE. The RR was 15% with median progression free survival 10.5 months. These findings demonstrate encouraging tolerability of alrizomadlin monotherapy with antitumor activity in patients with TP53 wild type SGC, especially ACC.

sec.p: Subject terms: Head and neck cancer, Cancer, Clinical trials

abstract.p: Preclinical studies have evaluated murine double minue 2 (MDM2) inhibitors as a treatment for adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC). Here the authors present a phase I clinical trial reporting tolerability and efficacy preliminary data for the MDM2 inhibitor alrizomadlin (APG-115) in patients with TP53 wild type salivary gland cancers, especially adenoid cystic carcinoma.

sec.p: Received 2025 Sep 26; Accepted 2026 Mar 2; Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Malignant salivary gland cancers (SGC) are a rare site of head and neck tumors accounting for ~6–8% of primary head and neck cancers1. Most patients present with localized disease and are treated with curative intent; however, a subset of patients develop metastatic disease. Once metastatic, treatment is palliative, and disease behavior is variable in so far as some patients have asymptomatic, indolent disease for years before growing rapidly and necessitating treatment. Results of historical trials in metastatic SGC are difficult to interpret given inclusion of patient with indolent disease. As such, contemporary studies have limited enrollment to patients with documented progressive disease2. Although often grouped together due to their rarity and anatomic location, malignant metastatic SGC encompass several distinct tumors of which the most common is adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC)3.

There are no approved systemic therapeutics for ACC. Cytotoxic chemotherapies and combinations have shown overall response rate (ORR) ranging 0-44% (albeit with unclear survival benefit)4, and multi-receptor vascular endothelilal growth receptor (VEGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors which have shown response rates ranging from 0-15% and a median progression free survival (PFS) of 5.7–17.5 months (mo)5–10. In a randomized trial, axitinib demonstrated an improvement in mPFS (5.7 vs 2.8 mo) versus observation with an ORR of only 9%5.

Other non-ACC salivary gland cancers include salivary ductal carcinoma, acinic cell carcinoma, mucoepidermoid carcinoma, and mammary analog secretory carcinoma. Although some of these tumors may have targetable molecular alterations including androgen receptor overexpression, HER2 amplification and/or overexpression, or rarely actionable genomic alterations (i.e., NTRK fusions), treatment options are limited with no approved systemic agents. Recognizing that a survival benefit is seen despite a lack of overt radiographic response, contemporary studies have pivoted to the use of PFS as the primary efficacy endpoint for trials in SGC especially ACC2.

Mutations in the TP53 gene are the most common molecular alteration in solid tumors but TP53 is frequently unaltered in SGC. The p53 protein is a potent transcription factor that plays a prominent role in many human malignancies. In cells containing wild- type p53, MDM2 is the cellular protein responsible for the negative regulation of p53 transactivation via an autoregulatory feedback mechanism. When activated, p53 transcribes the MDM2 gene leading to production of the MDM2 protein. MDM2 proceeds to directly bind to p53, which inhibits the function of p53 via several mechanisms11,12. MDM2 gene amplifications are a common event in SGCs, particularly prevalent in ACC13–15. MDM2 inhibition has been of particular interest in SGC as a mechanism to restore p53 function. MI-773 previously was shown to mediate ACC tumor regression in patient-derived xenograft models of ACC as both a single agent as well as potential synergy when administered in combination with platinum chemotherapy16,17. Alrizomadlin is a potent oral small-molecule MDM2 inhibitor, which shows significant cell growth inhibitory activity in vitro at low nanomolar concentrations and was previously evaluated in a first in human clinical trial in advanced solid tumors. Given these data, we hypothesized that alrizomadlin would have significant clinical activity in TP53 wildtype (TP53wt) SGC.
In this work, we conducted a phase I clinical trial to evaluate the safety and antitumor activity of alrizomadlin +/- carboplatin in patients with progressive TP53wt SGC.

sec.title: Patient and disease characteristics
sec.p: Forty-one patients were enrolled between October 2019 and February 2024. Forty patients received at least one dose of drug and were evaluable for DLT (Fig. 1). Baseline characteristics for 40 enrolled patients evaluable for toxicity are shown in (Table 1). Median age was 59 years (range: 33–76), 26 patients were female (65%), and the majority had ACC (n = 31, 78%). Fourteen patients (35%) had previous palliative systemic therapy for locoregionally recurrent or metastatic salivary gland cancer, of which six patients had previous VEGFR TKI exposure. The median number of prior lines of therapy was 2 (range 1-7). All patients had PD by imaging at baseline, with one patient having new metastatic disease. All other patients had > 20% increase in tumor burden within 12 months of enrollment (median: 55.8%, range: 21.7% to 300%). Of the 27 patients who had scans available in the previous 6 months, 25 patients (93%) had a > 20% increase.

sec.title: Dose finding and dose limiting toxicities
sec.p: During the study, among the 40 patients evaluable for toxicity, four patients experienced DLTs (three in the monotherapy arm, one in the combination arm). Amongst patients in the monotherapy arm, DLTs included two cases of grade 4 neutropenia and one instance of grade 3 dizziness. Among these three patients, one DLT occurred during cycle 1 and two occurred during cycle 2. In the combination arm, one patient experienced neutropenic fever (grade 3) with associated anemia (grade 3) and neutropenia (grade 4) during cycle 1. For all cases, DLTs resolved and patients were able to resume treatment at a reduced dose.

Dose de-escalation was not recommended by the TITE-CRM for alrizomadlin monotherapy and all patients were treated at the highest dose level (150 mg). The number of observed DLTs and the estimated posterior probability of toxicity at the three dose levels are shown in Supplementary Fig. Table 1. The dose level of alrizomadlin monotherapy closest to the target probability of 30% was 150 mg, which was determined to be the MTD.

sec.title: Toxicity, dose reductions, and reasons for discontinuation
sec.p: Treatment with alrizomadlin monotherapy was tolerated relatively well with 3 patients (9.1%) discontinuing due to treatment related AEs (TRAEs). Seventeen (52%) patients came off therapy due to progression, 4 (12%) due to physician discretion, and 4 (12%) due to patient withdrawal of consent. A total of 17 patients (52%, 13 monotherapy, 4 combination) required at least one dose modification. Ten patients underwent one dose reduction to 100 mg (all monotherapy), and 3 patients underwent two dose reductions to 50 mg. The most common grade 3 TRAEs included fatigue (22%), thrombocytopenia (19%), neutropenia (17%), and nausea (11%) (Table 2). Grade 4 myelosuppression (neutropenia and thrombocytopenia) was observed in four patients (11%).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Thirty-four response-evaluable patients were treated with alrizomadlin monotherapy. Among the first stage of 14 patients treated with alrizomadlin monotherapy (Arm A), there were 2 responses thereby allowing for enrollment to the second stage. Five patients (14.7%) had a confirmed partial response (PR), and 27 had a best response of stable disease (SD) (79.4%), amounting to a disease control rate (DCR) of 94.1% (Table 3). Two patients (5.9%) had a best response of progressive disease (PD). The median follow-up time for PFS was 15.0 months. The 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) was 69.8% (95% CI: 55.7, 87.3) with a median PFS of 9.3 months (95% CI: 7.4, 14.0). The median duration of therapy was 7.8 months (range 1.3–31.5) and as of 5/08/25, 3 patients were still on active therapy as of the data cut-off as shown in the swimmer’s plot (Fig. 2). Twenty-six patients (76.5%) showed reductions in tumor sizes during follow-up as shown in Fig. 3.

sec.p: A planned analysis of the efficacy of alrizomadlin monotherapy in patients with ACC (n = 25) versus non-ACC (n = 9) was undertaken to best identify populations deriving benefit from therapy. Among patients with ACC, five (20.0%) had a confirmed PR and 19 had a best response of SD (76.0%) amounting to a DCR of 96.0%. The 6-month PFS was 75.0% (95% CI: 59.5, 94.5) with a median PFS of 9.7 months (95% CI: 8.1, 18.6) (Fig. 4). In non-ACC patients, no patients had a confirmed PR and 8 had a best response of SD (88.9%). The 6-month PFS was 55.6% (95% CI: 31.0, 99.7) with a median PFS of 7.4 months (95% CI: 4.6, not evaluable (NE)). There was no statistically significant difference in PFS between the two groups (log-rank p = 0.69); however, small group sizes limit the power to detect between-group differences.

sec.title: Alrizomadlin + carboplatin
sec.p: Four patients were enrolled to alrizomadlin + carboplatin (Arm B) prior to closure of the combination arm, all of whom had ACC (Supplementary Fig. Table 2). One patient had a confirmed PR and the other three had a best response of SD. The 6-month PFS was 75% (95% CI: 43, 100) with a median PFS of 19.8 months (95% CI: 4.8, NE) (Supplementary Figs. 1, 2). Among patients treated with the combination of alrizomadlin and carboplatin there was a higher rate of grade 3 and 4 TRAEs (Supplementary Figs. Table 3). Grade 4 TRAEs included neutropenia (n = 2) as well as thrombocytopenia (n = 1) and the most common grade 3 TRAEs included thrombocytopenia (n = 3), neutropenia (n = 2), and anemia (n = 2). Four patients underwent two dose reductions to 50 mg.

sec.title: Translational studies
sec.p: Targeted genomic sequencing of 18 salivary gland tumors, comprising 14 ACC and 4 non-ACC tumors, revealed a low frequency of somatic mutations (Fig. 5). In the ACC group, each of these genes PTEN, NTRK1, MET, BRCA2, FGFR4 harbored a missense mutation in a single tumor (1/14; 7.1%), and a nonsense mutation was identified in SETD2, also in one ACC tumor (1/14, 7.1%). In the non-ACC group, a single missense mutation was detected in MTOR in one of four tumors (1/4, 25%). Importantly, no mutations were identified in TP53 in either ACC or non-ACC tumors, confirming that all samples were TP53wt. In addition, no mutations were detected in MDM2 or MDM4 in any tumor.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Viable treatments for metastatic SGC, particularly ACC, are an area of significant unmet need. Previous preclinical data have shown the potent antitumor activity of MDM2 inhibition in ACC patient-derived xenograft models when used alone or in combination with chemotherapy providing the basis for this phase I clinical trial assessing alrizomadlin +/- carboplatin in patients with radiographically progressive TP53wt SGC16,17.

Data from this study indicate that alrizomadlin monotherapy is well tolerated at identified doses in patients with metastatic TP53wt SGC. The rate of discontinuation due to TRAE was 9%, which is comparable to the rates observed in other current trials assessing axitinib and lenvatinib (12-15%), as was the rate of grade 3 or 4 TRAEs in our trial and previous studies6,7,10. Although palliative treatments necessitate careful consideration of toxicity profiles, both agents remain widely used for the management of metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma despite the occurrence of serious toxicities. Four DLTs were reported—three in the monotherapy arm and one in the combination arm. This is largely attributed to the conservative definition of the DLT window (set at two cycles), which was more stringent than those in most early-phase clinical trials of targeted agents, especially for patients treated with alrizomadlin alone. Only one DLT occurred during the first cycle, aligning with the rates observed with agents that progress to advanced clinical development. Importantly, all patients were able to resume therapy at a reduced dose.

Efficacy results from this study indicate a significant signal of activity, particularly in ACC in which response and survival outcomes are comparable to those found in recent studies on modern VEGFR TKIs. Confirmed ORR for single-agent lenvatinib or axitinib typically range from 0-15%, and up to 18% for axitinib in combination with avelumab5,7,8,10. In this study, alrizomadlin monotherapy achieved a confirmed ORR of 20% in ACC. Early data from a phase II trial of alrizomadlin +/- toripalimab in advanced solid tumors further corroborates these results, reporting a similar response rate of 20% in an independent ACC cohort18. Additionally, the responses and disease stabilization observed in our trial were durable, with a median response duration of 16.1 months and a disease stabilization period of 8.5 months. In ACC, treatment responses are often noted through improvements in progression-free survival (PFS) rather than traditional RECIST responses2. Contemporary trials with axitinib and lenvatinib have reported median PFS ranging from 5.7-10.8 months, although their findings are constrained by single-arm phase II designs5–8. A randomized study comparing observation and axitinib showed a median PFS of 2.8 months versus 10.8 months, though interpretation is complicated due to the crossover design5. Both axitinib and lenvatinib are recommended for treating recurrent/metastatic ACC19.

In this study, alrizomadlin monotherapy resulted in a median PFS of 9.6 months. While cross-trial comparisons have limitations, these survival outcomes are similar to those of other effective agents. Although interpreting disease stabilization and PFS in single-arm phase II studies can be difficult due to variable disease behaviors, it is notable that all patients demonstrated objective progression before enrollment, and 76% experienced a reduction in tumor burden. Together, these findings further support the antitumor activity of alrizomadlin monotherapy

Previous work suggested that combined MDM2 inhibition plus platinum chemotherapy would offer potent antitumor activity in TP53wt ACC. In this study, the combination of alrizomadlin and carboplatin was quite toxic. Although only four patients were enrolled in this cohort before it was closed because of safety concerns there was one DLT, 50% of patients had grade 4 toxicities, and 100% had grade 3 TRAEs primarily driven by the carboplatin. Intriguingly, 1 of the 4 patients had a partial response which was quite sustained (27 months), and a median PFS of 19.8 months. This trial was originally designed with therapeutic dose levels of both alrizomadlin and carboplatin. Given the preclinical suggestion of synergy, this leads to the intriguing question as to whether subtherapeutic doses of carboplatin or other chemotherapy medications may offer the added clinical benefit without added toxicities.

This study should be interpreted with limitations. It was designed as a phase I trial to assess the safety/tolerability of alrizomadlin +/- chemotherapy in patients with radiographically progressive metastatic SGCs as it was unknown if there was going to be a unique safety signal in this population. Although there was a protocol defined prespecified subgroup analyses to assess progression-free survival as well as treatment response based on histology (i.e., ACC vs. non-ACC), the trial was not powered to evaluated improvement in survival outcomes compared to historical outcomes. Although the study was not powered to make formal conclusions regarding PFS, we believe that our sample size of patients with ACC coupled with our mature PFS data supports a signal of activity. We also recognize that several contemporary studies required >20% or clinical progression within 6 months whereas our eligibility stipulated progression within 12 months. Our eligibility criteria required radiographic PD and were less subjective than previous studies in which clinical progression was acceptable for eligibility. Although not all patients had scans available within a 6-month window, 93% of those with available imaging showed >20% progression. Furthermore, we believe that a strength of our study is the mature follow-up, enrollment of patients across several diverse institutions, and expert review of pathology confirming the diagnosis of all patients.

In summary, alrizomadlin monotherapy shows promising antitumor activity and is well-tolerated in patients with TP53 wild-type salivary gland cancer. The antitumor activity is particularly pronounced in those with adenoid cystic carcinoma. These encouraging results support the need for confirmatory trials to validate the clinical benefits for patients with metastatic ACC.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: The study (NCT03781986) was approved by the institutional review board at the University of Michigan Rogel Cancer Center as well as participating sites and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice Guidelines. This was an open-label, multicenter phase I trial conducted at the University of Michigan Rogel Cancer Center (UMCC, Ann Arbor, MI), H. Lee Moffitt Cancer Center (Tampa, Florida), and University of Chicago Cancer Center (Chicago, Illinois). All patients provided written informed consent before enrollment. Patients with histologically documented malignant salivary gland cancers non amenable to curative therapy were eligible if they met the following criteria; previous mutational testing demonstrating no evidence of a TP53 mutation; presence of measurable disease by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1; ≥20% increase in tumor burden in the preceding 12 months per RECIST by treated physician assessment; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0 or 1; age ≥ 18 years old; able to take oral medications without breaking capsules; and adequate organ and bone marrow function. Any number of prior therapies was allowed. Exclusion criteria included prior treatment with an MDM-2 inhibitor, active brain metastases, or progressive disease within 6 months of the last dose of platinum-based chemotherapy. Complete eligibility criteria can be found in the study protocol (online only). Participants were not compensated for participation. Patient sex was collected and based on self-reporting, gender was not collected. The cut-off date for analysis was May 8, 2025.

sec.title: Study procedures
sec.p: Doses were assigned using the time-to-event continual reassessment method (TITE-CRM), which continuously estimates the probability of dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) and assigns patients to the dose closest to but not exceeding the estimated target rate of 30% using a one-parameter logistic regression and Bayesian modeling20,21. The acute observation period for DLT comprised the first two cycles of treatment, constituting a 42-day time period. The initial dose level for alrizomadlin was 150 mg, which could be decreased to 100 or 50 mg.

Alrizomadlin was administered orally every other day, days 1–14 in 21-day cycles. Starting dose level was recommended by Ascentage Pharma based on safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics from a previously completed first in human study (NCT02935907)22. Dose adherence was monitored by pill diaries. In patients treated with both carboplatin and alrizomadlin, carboplatin was also administered on day 1, with a starting dose level utilizing an area under the curve dose of 4.5 and alrizomadlin 150 mg (Supplementary Fig. Table 2). Treatment was continued until disease progression, intercurrent illness precluding further treatment, unacceptable adverse events (AEs), death, withdrawal of consent, or at the treating physician’s discretion. Imaging was obtained once every 6 weeks for the first six cycles, then extended to every 9 weeks.

sec.title: Dose-limiting toxicity
sec.p: Non-hematologic DLTs were defined as ≥ grade 3 non-hematological AEs, excluding nausea, vomiting, diarrhea; ≥ grade 3 nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea uncontrolled by maximal antiemetic/antidiarrheal therapy; any AE which in the judgment of the investigator was considered a DLT; grade 3 ALT and/or AST elevation. Hematologic DLTs were defined as thrombocytopenia of ≥ grade 3 if associated with clinically significant bleeding; ≥ grade 3 anemia lasting ≥7 days; grade 4 thrombocytopenia lasting ≥7 days; grade 4 neutropenia lasting 7 days or more; ≥ grade 3 neutropenia with a temperature of at least 38.5 °C; or ≥ grade 3 neutropenia with ≥ grade 3 infection.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) for MYB was performed using pS11-MYB (clone #EP769Y). MYB scoring was conducted by a board-certified head and neck pathologist (JBM) who determined the percentage of positive tumor nuclei.

ALDH1A1 staining was performed as previously described23, with the addition of 0.1% Tween 20 in the wash buffer. Briefly, slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated and boiled at 95 °C in citrate buffer for 20 min. Sections were permeabilized with Triton X-100, 3% hydrogen peroxides, blocked with avidin/biotin (Vector Laboratories) and background sniper (Biocare Medical). ALDH1A1 (1:1000), 4 °C, O/N was detected using Mach3 probe and Mach 3M-polymer-HRP, and stained with Betazoid DAB Chromagen kit (Biocare Medical). Slides were counterstained with Hematoxylin (Vector Laboratories). ALDH1A1 quantification was performed by a board-certified oral and maxillofacial pathologist (FN) using I-score values, which combine staining intensity and percentage of positivity, were obtained using Aperio ImageScope (Leica Biosystems). This was followed by a descriptive analysis of staining localization in tumor cells versus stroma, and cytoplasm versus cell membrane.

The correlation between ALDH1A1 staining quantification and PFS was assessed. The correlation coefficient was calculated for all individuals with available tissue who completed treatment at the time of analysis. Analysis was performed using R v4.3.1.

sec.title: DNA sequencing
sec.p: DNA extraction from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens was conducted as previously detailed24,25. A board- certified head and neck pathologist (J.B.M.) identified the tumor areas. Both tumor and adjacent normal tissue cores were collected, and genomic DNA was extracted using the Qiagen Allprep DNA/RNA FFPE kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The DNA was quantified with a Qubit, following the methodology previously described24. Subsequently, the DNA samples were sent to the University of Michigan Advanced Genomics core for library preparation and sequencing.

sec.title: Targeted capture sequencing library and analysis
sec.p: A minimum of 100 ng of genomic DNA from both tumor and adjacent normal tissue isolations was utilized for library preparation using the Rubicon DNA Thruplex (Rubicon Genomics, Ann Arbor, MI, USA) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Targeted capture was subsequently performed with our Nextera custom capture library, which includes 7814 high-density probes covering the coding exons of 233 genes. Next-generation sequencing was carried out on an Illumina NovaSeqXPlus (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) using the paired-end 151-bp reads.

sec.title: Quality control, variant calling and copy number analysis
sec.p: Raw sequencing reads were first assessed for quality using FastQC (v0.11.9). Trimming of low-quality bases and adapter sequences was performed using Trimgalore (v0.6.7) with default parameters. The filtered reads were then aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38) using BWA-MEM (v0.7.17). Alignment files were processed with SAMtools (v1.12) to convert SAM to BAM format and sort reads by coordinate. Duplicate reads were identified and marked using Picard-tools (v3.0.0). After marking duplicates, GATK (v4.3.0.0) was used for BQSR following best practices. The BaseRecalibrator tool was applied using known variant databases (dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, and Mills indels), followed by application of recalibrated scores with ApplyBQSR. Variants were identified using VarScan2 (v2.4.6) in somatic mode. The resulting variant call format file was annotated using ANNOVAR (v9.2019) to map functional annotations, including gene information, variant consequences, population allele frequencies, etc. This was followed by filtering the variants in the introns and intergenic regions. Variants with a minimum of five reads supporting the alternate allele in the tumor samples were considered as potential positives. Next, Copy number alterations were estimated using CNVkit (v0.9.12). CNVkit was run in batch mode using the pooled normal samples as a reference to calculate log2 copy number ratios for each tumor sample. Mutation and clinical data visualization, including oncoplots, was performed using maftools (v2.18.0) in R.

sec.title: Statistics and reproducibility
sec.p: The co-primary endpoints were determination of the DLT/maximally tolerated dose (MTD) as well as ORR per RECIST 1.1 for alrizomadlin monotherapy +/- carboplatin. Planned protocol specified secondary endpoints included safety via CTCAE v 5.0, survival endpoints (overall survival, PFS, duration of response (DOR)), and ORR by tumor histology (ACC vs. non-ACC). Evaluation of survival endpoints based on histologic subtype (ACC vs non-ACC) was performed as a non-protocol-specified exploratory analysis. The study was initially designed to enroll 62 response-evaluable patients in two phases (42 in the first phase (14 in Arm A- alrizomadlin monotherapy, 28 in Arm B- alrizomadlin + carboplatin), then an additional 20 in the arm with the best response rate). After 4 patients were enrolled in Arm B, the trial design was modified to a single-arm study of alrizomadlin monotherapy after safety meetings noted increased toxicities in the combination arm. The revised sample size was 34 response-evaluable patients in Arm A total (Fig. 7). If less than two responses (partial or complete) were seen in the first stage, the trial would be stopped however if two or more responses were seen in the first 14 evaluable patients treated with APG-115 monotherapy, enrollment would continue with enrollment of the additional 20 patients. Using a 1-sided exact test of binomial proportions and an α = 0.05, we defined MTD as the dose level assigned to the next patient if a new patient were to be enrolled (i.e., the highest dose level for which the estimated posterior probability of toxicity is ≤30%). Adverse events were summarized at the patient level using the highest grade when multiple AEs were present for the same category. Overall survival was defined as the time from the start of treatment to death, with censoring at the last follow-up. Progression-free survival was defined as the time from start of treatment to the earlier of progression or death, with censoring at the time of transition to new therapy if within 8 weeks of the last imaging assessment, or time of the last imaging assessment. Time-to-event endpoints were summarized using the Kaplan–Meier method.

J.C.B. and A.B. performed and interpreted analyses of DNA sequencing. J.M.H. reviewed all tissue samples to confirm diagnosis and isolate tumor tissue for translational analysis, and performed scoring for MYB. K.W., F.N., and J.E.N. performed staining, scoring, statistical analysis, and interpretation of ALDH1A1 translational data. K.I. was the translational specimen manager. Y.Z. and T.F. contributed to protocol development. P.L.S. was the principal investigator and wrote the protocol, enrolled patients, supervised translational analyses, and wrote the paper. All authors edited and approved the paper.
